1:
The word rendered burden is discussed by three voices and defended by one. Gill reports that it covers prophecies both sorrowful and joyful, that it is called a burden because the word of the Lord is often burdensome to carnal men, and that it may also be rendered a declaration or publication, the Arabic version giving it as a revelation. Calvin prefers to keep the burden and argues against those who render it prophecy: the phrase the prophecy of the word would be strange and without meaning, whereas the burden of the word of the Lord flows well and reminds us that the word would not be ineffectual but would lie on these nations as a weight they could not shake off. Henry works the metaphor as far as it will go, that those are miserable on whom the burden of the word rests, since it is a weight they can neither shake off nor bear up under, and that whom the wrath of God makes its mark it will surely hit. Keil and Delitzsch put the heading structurally instead, as the mark that this and a later oracle are corresponding portions of a greater whole, the two together treating the war between the heathen world and Israel from opposite sides.

Clarke uses the opening of the chapter to reproduce an argument that these chapters are not this prophet's at all. He reports that most learned men assign them rather to another prophet or to someone before the captivity, and gives the case: the first eight chapters are expressly assigned, connected with one another, pertinent to their occasion and uniform in style, whereas these are not expressly assigned, are unconnected with what precedes, are in many parts unsuitable to the time, have a more adorned and poetical turn, and break the unity of the book; and he adds the well-known citation of a passage from these chapters under another prophet's name. He then states his own conclusion, that they form not only a distinct work but belong to a different and unknown author. Nobody else in the chapter raises the question. Ellicott instead reports a discovery that removes an old difficulty, that the place-name which had been an insuperable trouble to commentators is now known from Assyrian inscriptions to have been a town or district near Damascus and Hamath. Wesley and Henry both take it simply for Syria, Henry admitting that it does not appear why the country was so called.

The clause about the eye is where the renderings diverge most. Ellicott canvasses several and prefers that the eye of man, and of all the tribes of Israel, will be directed to the Lord, so that when the judgments are fulfilled the eyes of all are turned to him in wonder; he records the old Greek's quite different construction, which makes the Lord's eye rest on man, and a proposal to read Syria for man on the ground that two Hebrew letters are easily interchanged. Clarke gives the same alternative as an easy sense followed by the versions, that the eye of the Lord is over man and over all the tribes. Henry offers both and draws a moral from each: on the first, that it is a sign God is about to appear for his people when he raises their expectations from him; on the second, that he is King of nations as well as of saints and will therefore punish the sins of other peoples too. Wesley reads it as an appeal, that those wronged by Syrian injustice look to heaven for right. Gill and Calvin keep to the comfort rather than the grammar, Calvin observing that the doctrine is consolation to the godly, who may know they are safe under the protection of one who carries on war with their enemies.
2:
The northern city is placed and then given a surprising afterlife. Keil and Delitzsch identify it on the Orontes under its modern name and explain the syntax, that the relative clause ties it to Damascus and separates it from the names that follow, so that the two together stand for Syria while the next pair are the two capitals of Phoenicia, joined by the clause about wisdom. Ellicott renders it that the burden falls even upon the city bordering on Damascus, and marks the transition, that so far the oracle has concerned Syria and now turns to the coast. Clarke names the same river. Wesley says the place was so near the storm that it should not quite escape, and takes the wisdom ascribed to the coastal cities as subtlety, each thinking by craft to save itself while God derides their wisdom. Gill alone goes further: he reports that one ancient authority identified this city with Antioch and that a Targum renders it so, and, if that is right, finds a resting-place of the word of the Lord there in a better sense, since the gospel was preached in that city, many were converted, a church of Jews and Gentiles was formed, and the disciples were first called Christians there.

When the doom fell is the flat disagreement of this tile. Ellicott concedes that the terms used of Syria are so general that, standing alone, they would leave us at a loss to fix the era, and then argues that the case is quite different with the island city: though besieged by one Assyrian king and perhaps taken by the Babylonian, it was certainly never devoured with fire until Alexander, who, as the historian records, having slain all but those who fled to the temples, ordered the houses to be set on fire; and since at the same time a detachment was sent against Syria, Ellicott refers the whole prophecy to that date. Clarke argues the contrary twice over. These prophecies, he says, are more suitable to an earlier prophet's days, since there is no evidence that Damascus was destroyed at any point between this prophet's time and the coming of Christ, Alexander having taken it without bloodshed, and since the coastal cities had lately been destroyed by the Babylonian it is not likely they could soon undergo another devastation; and at the verse about the smiting he states it plainly, that although Alexander did take these cities, the prediction seems to have been fulfilled by the earlier conqueror.

The stronghold and the wealth are treated as literal fact and then turned. Gill describes the city as built on a rock and a fortress by nature, from which he says it had its name, with a wall a hundred and fifty feet high and of an answering breadth; and he draws the double conclusion that it could defend itself neither against Alexander, who took it, nor against the gospel, which found its way in and was mighty to pull down strongholds in a spiritual sense. Keil and Delitzsch render the heaping of silver like dust and gold like the dirt of the streets without comment. On the sentence itself the two shortest notes disagree. Wesley takes the verb strictly, that she is cast out of her inheritance, which he says is what the word properly means. Gill reports the opposite construction from the old Greek, which makes the Lord inherit her, so that being converted she would become his possession and her riches be devoted to his service.
5:
The fear of the Philistine cities is given a different cause by each voice. Gill follows a Jewish commentator in making it imitation, that seeing the great city submit they submit too, and converts it into a spiritual sense, her wisdom not standing before the gospel; he notes the place did become Christian, a bishop of it sitting in the great council. Ellicott keeps it military and fills in what the histories omit: two cities are not named in connection with the march but must have been occupied, and the third was taken after a five-month siege, a contemporary writer mentioning its king brought alive to the conqueror. Clarke uses the verse for his authorship argument, that all these prophecies seem fulfilled before this prophet's own days, another sign that these chapters were not written by him.

The bastard who dwells in Ashdod produces four readings. Gill reports that some take the word as the name of a people, some understand Alexander, who gave out that he was not his mother's husband's son but a god's, and others the Maccabean leader who burnt the place with its temple. Clarke commits to Alexander, since his mother told a story of a god entering her apartment in the shape of a dragon, and asks whether her husband could have believed it; he adds that the word signifies a stranger. Ellicott takes it not of a person but of a mixed race, connecting it with a policy of breaking up nationalities and fusing peoples. Wesley agrees strangers are meant, having no right of inheritance.

The blood taken out of the mouth is read either literally or ritually. Gill notes that three versions make it their blood rather than his, and offers two senses, that they should no more thirst after blood, or no longer eat what was sacrificed to their gods. Clarke takes it as the Philistines abstaining from blood once incorporated with Israel, citing the historian for many becoming proselytes. Wesley keeps both, the delight in shedding blood and the abominable sacrifices they feasted on. Ellicott takes the abominations as idolatrous sacrifices and works at the comparison that follows. He canvasses three views of the Jebusite, that the word means Jerusalem, that it designates the remnant of the old tribes kept for servile duties, or that it means the people who dwelt with Judah in Jerusalem as equals and not as a conquered race; he prefers the last because the word stands parallel with the term for governor rather than contrasted with it. He then makes a historical admission the others do not: nothing is known of any great conversion of Philistines at this time, and later they still appear hostile, after which they vanish as a separate nation, probably having become indistinguishable from their neighbours.

The encamping about the house Clarke refers to a particular episode, the conqueror met by the high priest in his sacred robes, sparing what he had purposed to destroy and remitting the seventh-year tax because the law forbade cultivation then. Ellicott allows the promise was fulfilled at that entry but resists tying the phrase about passing and returning to that march, as one modern does, since the expression occurs elsewhere generally; and the word rendered army, so pointed in the Hebrew, is made a garrison by some who alter the vocalisation and a column by the old Greek. Gill takes the army for the persecutors who rose against the church in the first ages, and the encamping for a defence by angels, by ministers, and chiefly by God's presence. Keil and Delitzsch state the turn plainly: while the heathen world falls under judgment and its remnant is converted, the Lord protects his house and causes the King to appear. On the closing clause Ellicott adds the sharpest remark here, that in the estimation of the man of little faith God only sees when he actively interferes.
9:
That this verse is a prophecy of the Messiah is agreed by everyone, and the agreement is unusual for this chapter. Henry says it is plain from the literal accomplishment recorded in two Gospels and their express application of it, and enlarges on the title of king, a sovereign prince whose glory shines in Zion; he turns the coming into a call to expectancy, the king long in coming but now at the door, so that a few ages more will run out and he who is to come will come. Clarke argues negatively: it cannot be the governor of the return, who was never a king, and no king has ruled that people from the last of the old dynasty to his own day except Jesus. Gill takes the daughter addressed neither for the inhabitants generally nor the children who cried in the temple courts but for the church and true believers, and asks a rejoicing spiritual rather than external. Wesley glosses the epithets briefly, the righteous one who came to fulfil all righteousness and has salvation for all who believe.

The epithets themselves are rendered variously. Ellicott would translate the second not as having salvation but as saved, the third not as lowly but as afflicted. Henry records that some render the same clause as saving himself, rising out of the grave by his own power and so qualifying himself to be a saviour, though his own account is that the king has salvation to bestow on his subjects. Clarke keeps the received sense, that he alone saves from sin and death. On the animal ridden, Ellicott notes that the Hebrew is literally of she-asses, that riding so did not in the later period denote high rank as it had earlier, and that it cannot be proved to symbolise peace or humility here, though it does indicate absence of pomp. Clarke explains it differently: the kings had been commanded not to multiply horses, so entering on a horse would have broken a positive command, while the ass fulfilled the prophecy and kept the precept.

Ellicott then takes up the question the fulfilment raises. He says without hesitation that the act was performed deliberately in view of this prophecy, not merely to fulfil it but as a symbolic correction of the false notions about the Messiah's mission held by friends and enemies; and he argues that deliberate intention does not lessen the value of the act as a fulfilment, since any man might have ridden into the city on an ass, but not any man amid the acclamations of a multitude whose hearts were already won, nor could any man have founded an almost universal religion. He adds that the wording is borrowed from one passage of another prophet rather than two more familiar ones, and infers that the nation was to enjoy a certain political independence when its king came, its military power having ended.

The cutting off of the chariot is read as the mode of the kingdom rather than as a separate promise. Gill notes that the chariot meant is the military one. Clarke states the principle, that no wars shall be employed to spread this kingdom, founded not by might nor by power but by the Spirit. Wesley says the king will need no external force, neither chariot nor bow nor sword having brought salvation to him, and none shall be mentioned in the day of his conquest. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same conclusion from the structure, that as the king's coming contains no sign of earthly exaltation so his kingdom will not be established by worldly power; the battle-bow stands for the war-chariots generally, and the two names given represent the formerly divided kingdoms, united again under the Messiah. Ellicott adds that the peace is spoken not only to his own people but to the nations, by setting up his kingdom among them.
11:
Who is addressed in the eleventh verse is settled three ways. Gill argues from the gender that the words are spoken not to Christ but to the congregation, and takes them as the Father's declaration to the church of the benefits she should receive by the death of the Son. Wesley says the opposite, that these are Christ's words to Jerusalem, and reads the covenant blood as his: God's covenant as made by him, Zion's as made for her, Christ's as made in him. Clarke takes the covenant historically, the one made with the patriarchs and ratified by the blood of many victims until the Messiah should shed his own, as the ancient sacrifices typified. Ellicott gives the barest gloss, that the person addressed is Zion and the phrase means by means or in consideration of. Keil and Delitzsch supply the verses without comment. On the pit the readings split the same way. Ellicott identifies it as Babylon and Wesley likewise, the Jews having perished there had God not visited them; Clarke widens it to the whole human race under the arrest of God's judgments, fast bound in sin and loosed by a mercy that died in their stead.

The stronghold and the prisoners of hope divide the voices between a historical and a spiritual reading, with one voice holding both. Ellicott is the most concrete: he would render the word not stronghold but the steepness of their own land, and takes the exhortation as addressed to those still in Babylon and urged to come forth, prisoners because still there and of hope because glorious promises are theirs if they will accept them; he supports the setting by a verse from an earlier chapter admitted on all sides to postdate the return. Gill canvasses the same options and rejects that one: those who stayed cannot be meant, since they were at liberty to leave by the decree and so were not prisoners at all, much less prisoners hoping for a deliverance they might have had; he prefers those who had returned and found their land full of straits, and better still those who about the Messiah's coming were waiting for the consolation of Israel. Henry holds both together, the returned exiles prisoners in effect and those who stayed prisoners in fact, and directs both to the Messiah set before them in the promise as their stronghold, which he says was the stronghold of the faithful long before his coming. Clarke drops the history and turns the verse into an appeal to conscience, that those shut up under a sense of guilt look to him who was delivered for their offences, hope leading to faith and faith to the blood of the covenant. On the double recompense Ellicott makes it compensation for the sufferings, Wesley twice as much good as evil suffered, and Clarke an abundance of peace.

The bow and the arrows are read by all as an image of one people armed with another, and the disagreement is over the target. Gill takes it spiritually, the bow being the apostles, whose ministrations struck the hearts of men and brought them into subjection to Christ, a bow of the Lord's own bending that abode in strength. Wesley keeps it military, the second name supplying warriors as a filled quiver supplies arrows, the enemy being the Greeks who had bought the Jews for slaves, against whom they took arms under the Maccabees, to whom Christ made good much of this promise. Ellicott agrees on the fulfilment and dates it, adds that the verbs should be future, the tense being the prophetic perfect, and concedes the prophet may have had no distinct notion of such distant events. Clarke breaks with them: the language is too strong for the trifling advantage gained over one Syrian king, and these words probably remain to be fulfilled against the present possessors of those countries.
14:
The appearing over them is rendered three ways by one voice and once by each of the others. Gill lays out the alternatives: that the Lord shall appear to them, as in the days of his flesh and after the resurrection; or over and upon them, as at the ascension and the descent of the Spirit; or for them, by giving strength and fortitude and prospering their labours. Ellicott prefers that on their behalf he shall manifest himself, and explains the quarter named as that from which the most violent storms came over the desert. Wesley makes the arrow the divine judgments, swift and sudden as lightning that runs from one horizon to the other in a moment, and reports that some find an allusion to the tempest at the giving of the law. Clarke reads the appearing as a shadowing and refreshing, like the cloud over the camp in the wilderness, calls the description sublime, and prints a Greek imitation of it.

Clarke then claims a discovery, that a fine image and an allusion to a particular fact in these two verses have escaped the notice of every commentator. The oriental bow, he explains, must be bent backwards before it can be strung; so one tribe is the recurved bow, the other the arrow laid on the string, discharged with the momentum of lightning and kindling in its course through the air; and he supports the last touch with a Latin poet's line about a missile that glows as it flies.

The drinking in the next verse produces a flat contradiction. Clarke states expressly that there is no intimation here of drinking the blood of enemies, as some barbarous nations did; the people hold a feast after the victory, banquet on the spoils, and pour libations of wine at the foot of the altar as the priests poured the blood of victims. Ellicott says the filling is with the blood of their enemies, like the bowls in which priests caught the victims' blood before sprinkling it on the corners of the altar. Wesley takes a middle course, the drinking at festivals where thanksgiving sacrifices are offered and the filling with the blood of those sacrifices. On the sling stones Ellicott would render that they trample on them in their valorous onslaught rather than subdue with them; Clarke notes that the sling was an ancient and powerful instrument, and Wesley recalls its one famous use. Gill leaves the weapons and reads the defending spiritually, the Lord a shield to the apostles amid a thousand snares. Keil and Delitzsch keep to the sequence of the promises, that it is through this victory over the world-power that Israel attains to glory, and note that the verb translated save in what follows cannot mean merely to help or deliver, which would affirm far too little after what has gone before.
16:
The stones of a crown draw out the antiquarian in Clarke. He construes the phrase as crowned stones erecting themselves, monuments raised after some deliverance which appear to lift themselves up and solicit the notice of every traveller who passes. He allows a second possibility, that they were anointed with oil and served as a rough altar thrown up to mark a victory, and defends it by the use of the same word elsewhere of the anointing oil. Then he carries the guess home to his own country, proposing that most of the upright pillars ranged in circles which pass for druidical remains were raised either to commemorate a triumph or to dignify the grave of some chieftain. Wesley wants none of this and compresses the clause to four words, that such people are precious in God's sight, with the ensign meaning simply a trophy; he glosses the saving as what a shepherd does for his sheep. Gill directs the promise forward instead, to those whom the apostles' preaching had conquered and subdued, and enumerates what they are rescued from: sin, the law, the wrath to come, and the grip of every enemy. Ellicott passes over all of it to record a literary observation, that here the vocabulary and the imagery of a flock make their entrance, and will govern much of what follows in this book.

Whose excellence the closing exclamation praises is the last quarrel of the chapter, and it turns on a pronoun. Gill eliminates three candidates before naming his own: not the territory, as one Jewish expositor supposed; not the teaching of the law, which is how the Targum took it; not the nation either; but the Messiah, and specifically his mediatorial excellence rather than the goodness proper to his nature or displayed in his providence, comprising what he carries in his heart toward his people and what he holds in his hands to give them. Ellicott answers with a single syllable of grammar, that the possessive refers to Israel, and improves the noun as well, preferring goodliness to goodness; the verb applied to the young men he would not translate as making cheerful but as causing to multiply. Keil and Delitzsch stand with him on the pronoun, referring it to the land, and render the promise that grain will make youths shoot up as new wine does maidens. Clarke declines to choose a direction at all, holding the excellence to be both intrinsic and bestowed, comeliness and purity belonging to the giver and imparted to the receivers alike; and he leaves the harvest imagery literal, young men invigorated by abundance and lifting their voices about divine mercies when the crop is gathered in.
